html:
Before a single object is built, the BA must know the process the org automates. This phase teaches you to document the as-is process in swimlane diagrams, identify waste and handoff gaps, design the to-be process with the business, and capture metrics that prove the new process is better. Business Process Mapping is 12% of the CBA exam, but its real weight is higher: every requirement you write in Phase 4 is born from a mapped process.

Learning Objectives

  • Document as-is processes with swimlane diagrams...
  • Identify waste, bottlenecks, and handoff gaps on a diagram...
  • Design the to-be process together with the business...
  • Capture process metrics: steps, actors, cycle time, handoffs...
  • Use the Process_Map__c object, ProcessMapService, and practice SOQL in the lab...
  • Translate each process change into a measurable requirement...

1. Why Process Mapping Is a BA Superpower

Stakeholders experience their process as a blur of habits, exceptions, and workarounds. The BA's job is to slow it into a picture everyone can agree on and change: a shared diagram showing who does what, in what order, and where handoffs happen. Once drawn, a process can be measured, criticized, simplified, and rebuilt — nothing happens to a process you cannot see.

Process mapping also protects the scope. The BrightLogistics sales team believes the lead journey is "submit, and we call them." The dispatchers know it is "submit, wait in inbox, get copied by dispatcher, re-type into the tracker, call." These two descriptions are different processes. The map forces the disagreement into the open in Discovery — where it belongs — instead of during UAT, where the rest of the team pretends the disagreement never happened.

2. Process Mapping Vocabulary: Triggers, Activities, Decisions, Outcomes

Every process map uses a small, consistent vocabulary. The trigger event is what starts the process — a lead arriving, a case being opened. Activities are the work steps, drawn as rectangles. Decisions are the branches, drawn as diamonds, with defined paths. Handoffs are where work moves from one actor to another, and where the value usually leaks. The outcome is where the process ends — a dispatched lead, an approved requirement.

The same vocabulary applies whether you draw in a tool, on a whiteboard, or in mermaid inside a markdown file, as this roadmap does. What matters is consistency: if the start and end elements of every map are named differently, nobody can compare two processes. Agree on the vocabulary once and reuse it everywhere.

3. As-Is Swimlane Diagrams

A swimlane diagram is the process map standard for the CBA. Each row or column is an actor — a person, role, or system — and activities sit in the lane of whoever performs them. Arrows are the flow, diamonds are the decisions. The swimlane's unique power is showing WHERE work happens, exposing the handoffs as work passes lane to lane.

mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Web form submitted] --> B{Dispatcher reads inbox}
  B -->|yes| C[Re-type lead into tracker]
  B -->|no, 1-2 days| D[Lead waits in inbox]
  C --> E[Follow-up call scheduled]
  D --> B

Mark pain points directly on the diagram with a warning symbol and a number, then keep a legend beneath the map: "1 - lead sits idle 1-2 days," "2 - manual re-keying." That legend becomes the list the to-be process must fix — the seed of the requirement set. Exercise 3.1 As-is swimlane in Phase 15 draws the full BrightLogistics as-is map.

4. Where a Process Starts and Ends

Start where value starts: the trigger event, the first moment the business interacts with the customer need. Do not start with "employee opens Excel" — that presumes the current tooling. Start with the arrival of the thing that matters, the lead. End where value ends: the delivered outcome, the moment the customer need is satisfied. For lead intake that outcome is a dispatched shipment, not "call made" — the call is an activity, the dispatch is the outcome.

The discipline of explicit start and end points has a practical payoff: if two analysts map the same process and disagree on start or end, one of them is mapping a different scope. Agreeing boundaries first prevents the classic disaster of one team mapping "lead to call" while the finance owner believes you are mapping "lead to invoice." Confirm boundaries with the process owner before drawing a rectangle.

5. Mapping the As-Is: The BrightLogistics Lead Intake

Draw the BrightLogistics as-is process exactly as it is observed, not as it is documented on paper. The web form drops submissions into a shared email inbox. The dispatcher on the morning shift reads new emails and re-types qualifying leads into a company tracker spreadsheet. A follow-up call happens within three days if the lead survived the queue. The process observation ends with two hard facts: 1-2 days of idle time inside the inbox, and full re-keying of every field.

The as-is map is not flattering and must not be sanitized. If customers complain twice about slow quotes, the map shows the second complaint as a rework loop, not a footnote. Recording reality — including the parts the business is ashamed of — is what makes the to-be promise credible. The process owner signs the as-is map as "this is how we work today," and that signature becomes the baseline every improvement is measured against.

6. Spotting Waste

The classic waste patterns in a business process are easy to spot once you have the map drawn. Check each pattern against the as-is diagram and mark what you find.

WasteProcess hintSalesforce fix
Re-keyingSame data typed twiceWeb-to-Lead, integration, prefill
WaitingLong idle between handoffsAssignment rules, notifications
ReworkDefects found lateValidation rules, guardrails
Over-processingManual steps add no valueFlows, auto-calc fields
Handoff gapNobody owns the next stepOwner fields, routing, RACI

BrightLogistics exhibits four of the five at once: re-keying (web form to tracker), waiting (inbox sleeps overnight), handoff gap (no owner between the inbox and the first call), and over-processing (manual transcription adds no value). Rework will soon appear in the form of duplicate leads and lost callbacks. Each marked pattern on the map is a candidate requirement in the to-be design, and Exercise 3.2 Waste walk in Phase 15 runs this audit formally.

7. Handoff Gaps and Ownership

A handoff gap is a point in the map where work stops having an owner. The email leaves the web form and no one is responsible until the morning shift reads it — that is a gap measured in hours. Handoff gaps are the most expensive and least visible waste because they appear in maps only as the space between lanes. The fix is always structural: an explicit owner from the moment the trigger fires.

On the to-be BrightLogistics map, the moment the web form submits, an assignment rule gives the lead a dispatcher owner, and a timer-driven escalation fields a nudge if nobody acts. The RACI of Phase 2 reinforced the same idea for people; the data model reinforces it for records. Every to-be step that exists to close a handoff gap earns its place on the map.

8. Process Metrics: Steps, Actors, Cycle Time, Handoff Count

A process map without numbers is a picture; with numbers it is an argument. Capture four baseline metrics on the as-is map before re-designing anything. Step count is the number of activities (excluding decisions); actor count is the number of lanes that do work; cycle time is the elapsed clock time from trigger to outcome; handoff count is the number of times work crosses between lanes. All four are measurable facts the diagram can be audited against.

apex
// ProcessMapService stores measurable facts on Process_Map__c
Process_Map__c pm = new Process_Map__c(
  Name               = 'Lead Intake',
  Step_Count__c      = 5,
  Actor_Count__c     = 2,
  Cycle_Time_Days__c = 4,
  Status__c          = 'As-Is Documented'
);

The BrightLogistics numbers are brutal: five steps, two actors, up to four days of cycle time, and at least one unowned handoff. These four numbers become the internal baseline and the checklist the to-be map is judged against. Exercise 3.3 Process metrics baseline in Phase 15 formalizes the calculation and evidence trail.

9. Measuring the As-Is to Prove the To-Be

Measure one concrete example, end to end, before you design the future state. Pick the single most recent lead, find its exact timestamps — submitted, read, entered in the tracker, first call, dispatched — and compute the cycle. The BrightLogistics example measures 4 days from inquiry to first call, matching the rough 48-hours-plus of the brief. One real example beats a hundred estimates, because the process owner has seen the actual record and cannot argue with it.

The measurement serves the KPI negotiation. The brief's target is a lead-to-dispatch cycle under 4 hours, down from roughly 48. To believe the to-be number, you need the as-is number decomposed: how many of those four days are waiting, how many are genuine work? Almost always waiting dominates, which is why automation that removes waiting delivers so fast.

10. Designing the To-Be Process

Draft the to-be map with the business, removing the re-keying and the waiting and leaving every step that genuinely adds value. The to-be BrightLogistics journey: web form submits a Lead record, a validation rule catches missing fields, an assignment rule routes it to the open dispatcher, a call task is created automatically, and a dashboard shows today's queue. One input, one owner, immediate action.

The design rule that keeps the to-be honest: if a step appears for a reason you cannot state out loud, it is waste in disguise. Every to-be step must earn its place by creating customer value or protecting a downstream step. When the business proposes keeping the tracker "just as a backup," challenge it: the requirement behind the backup is a reporting need, and reporting belongs to reports and dashboards, not a parallel data entry lane.

11. Validating the To-Be with the Process Owner

A to-be map is a proposal until the process owner signs it. Walk the owner through it lane by lane, asking at each handoff: who owns this step, what happens when it fails, and what is the reporting effect. The senior dispatcher review surfaces the "wrong carrier" fear as a real decision branch: routing criteria configure the rule, and a manual reassign action is the override path. The design is finished only when the accountable person agrees to be measured against it.

Signature discipline matters for one cynical reason: the signed to-be map is the change control document. When someone asks in sprint three "why did we build a manual reassign step?", the answer is a dated signature on the swimlane. The Process_Map__c record holds both maps (As_Is_Description__c, To_Be_Description__c) so the decision survives with a timestamp.

12. Translating Process Change into Requirements

Every to-be change is a requirement waiting to be written. Say the change in the language of the process, then in the language of the system: "Reduce lead-to-call cycle time from 4 days to 1" is a measurable business need; "auto-assign each inbound Lead an owner within 60 seconds" is its system-level translation. The first goes in the BRD goals; the second is a numbered functional requirement ready for Phase 4's approval flow.

The mapping between process and requirements is one-to-many. One to-be step usually produces several: the assignment step yields a functional requirement (assign), a data requirement (owner field), an automation requirement (Flow on create), and a reporting requirement (queue dashboard). Process maps that produce no requirements were not changed; they were redrawn.

13. The Lab: Process_Map__c, ProcessMapService, and Practice SOQL

The lab turns the phase into metadata. The Process_Map__c object (force-app/main/default/objects/Process_Map__c/) records Step_Count__c, Actor_Count__c, Cycle_Time_Days__c, Status__c, As_Is_Description__c, and To_Be_Description__c. ProcessMapService in force-app/main/default/classes/ProcessMapService.cls requires at least one step and one actor per map, enforces the status lifecycle (As-Is Documented, To-Be Drafted, Confirmed, Implemented), and flags maps whose cycle time contradicts their step count.

soql
// scripts/soql/process-maps.soql — audit the process portfolio
SELECT Name, Step_Count__c, Actor_Count__c, Cycle_Time_Days__c, Status__c
FROM Process_Map__c
WHERE Status__c = 'As-Is Documented'
ORDER BY Cycle_Time_Days__c DESC

Run the practice query with sf apex run --apex-code-file scripts/soql/process-maps.soql --target-org myDevOrg and you should see the exercise product: a confirmed as-is map with its baseline numbers and a to-be map awaiting owner sign-off. Two maps side by side as records are your evidence the process actually changed and the KPI is achievable — the reporting foundation Phase 11 fit-gap and Phase 12 UAT stand on.

Hands-On Exercises

Exercise 3.1: As-Is Swimlane of BrightLogistics Lead Intake

  1. Draw a swimlane diagram with two lanes: Web Form/Inbox and Dispatcher.
  2. Place the observed steps in order: form submitted, email lands in inbox, dispatcher reads inbox, lead re-typed into tracker, follow-up call.
  3. Draw a diamond for "dispatcher available to read the inbox today?" and show the waiting loop for the negative path.
  4. Mark each pain point with a warning symbol and number, then list the legend beneath the map.

Expected result: a two-lane swimlane showing the inbox as the bottleneck, with at least three numbered pain points. What it proves: you can draw the as-is honestly and locate waste visually. Pairs with Exercise 3.1 As-is swimlane in Phase 15.

Exercise 3.2: Waste-Walk Audit on Your Own Diagram

  1. Take the as-is map from Exercise 3.1 and run the five waste patterns against it: re-keying, waiting, rework, over-processing, handoff gap.
  2. For each waste found, name the Salesforce fix from the table in section 6.
  3. Score the process: how many of the five wastes are present?

Expected result: a waste-score sheet with at least four of the five detected and a fix named for each. What it proves: you translate observed friction into a specific remedy and requirement seed. Pairs with Exercise 3.2 Waste walk in Phase 15.

Exercise 3.3: Baseline the BrightLogistics Process Metrics

  1. Set the four baseline metrics from your map: step count, actor count, cycle time (48 hours minimum, use the observed 4 days), and handoff count.
  2. Create a Process_Map__c record with Status__c As-Is Documented and the numbers in their fields.
  3. Run scripts/soql/process-maps.soql and confirm your record appears in the ordered result.

Expected result: a Process_Map__c record whose four fields match your diagram, verified by the practice query. What it proves: the process baseline is a data fact, not a slide — auditable by anyone with SOQL access. This pairs with Exercise 3.3 Process metrics baseline in Phase 15.

Exercise 3.4: To-Be Swimlane and Requirement Translation

  1. Redraw the lead intake as the to-be: one lane for the system (form, assignment rule, call task), one for the dispatcher (own, call).
  2. Delete every step that does not earn its place, and state out loud why each surviving step exists.
  3. Write the requirement set the map produces: one functional, one data, one automation, one reporting requirement.
  4. Ask a partner to review the to-be map as the process owner and challenge one handoff.

Expected result: a to-be swimlane with no unearned steps and a four-item requirement set traceable to the map. What it proves: process change and requirements are the same work at two levels. Pairs with Exercise 3.4 To-be design in Phase 15.

Key Terms Glossary

TermDefinition
Trigger eventThe moment that starts a process, such as a lead arriving or a requirement being submitted.
Swimlane diagramA process map where each lane is an actor and handoffs appear as flows between lanes.
ActivityA work step performed by one actor, drawn as a rectangle on a process map.
DecisionA branch in the process, drawn as a diamond, with defined paths for each outcome.
HandoffThe point where work passes from one actor to another; a common spot for waste.
As-is processThe current process exactly as observed, before any improvement.
To-be processThe redesigned target process, agreed and signed by the process owner.
Re-keyingWaste where the same data is typed twice into different systems.
Cycle timeThe elapsed clock time from trigger event to delivered outcome.
Process ownerThe accountable person who signs the as-is and to-be maps as correct.
Process metricsBaseline facts — steps, actors, cycle time, handoffs — proving improvement.
Requirement seedA to-be step restated as a measurable requirement.

Certification Checkpoints

  • I can draw an as-is swimlane diagram with trigger, activities, decisions, and outcome.
  • I can name the five classic wastes and their Salesforce fixes.
  • I can identify a handoff gap on a map and its owner-less point.
  • I can compute step count, actor count, cycle time, and handoff count from a diagram.
  • I can design a to-be map where every step earns its place.
  • I can get a process owner to sign the to-be map and know why the signature matters.
  • I can restate every process change as a measurable requirement.
  • I can create a Process_Map__c record and query it with practice SOQL.

Summary

You learned to document the current process as an as-is swimlane, spot the five wastes and handoff gaps where value leaks, and capture the four baseline metrics that make a process map an argument instead of a picture. You designed a to-be process with the business, got it signed by its owner, and translated every change into measurable requirements — storing both maps on Process_Map__c and auditing them with ProcessMapService and practice SOQL.
